covers.quote: Set up grammatical structure for list items with a lead-in.
Use a heading, not a lead-in.
A stand-alone list has no lead-in, only a heading.

rules.quote: All lists have a 'lead-in' (a phrase or sentence) or heading to introduce the list.
rules.violation_condition: A displayed list has neither a lead-in nor a heading, or a stand-alone list uses a lead-in instead of a heading.
when: A sentence list may have a heading, sentence lead-in or phrase lead-in.
A fragment list has a phrase or sentence lead-in.
A stand-alone list requires a heading rather than a lead-in.
rules.why: G-2 combines the introductory structure requirements and the stand-alone exception; G-4 absorbs the restatements.

covers.quote: Lists are only for a series of items.

rules.quote: Don’t use a list if you have only one item.
rules.violation_condition: A list contains only one item.
rules.why: G-4 treats the following explanation as a restatement of the single-item prohibition.

covers.quote: Move long lists to a separate page or an appendix.

rules.quote: Make short lists
rules.specification: The page does not define a long list or give an item-count threshold. The relocation instruction is treated as the remedy for a long list, not a second finding.
rules.violation_condition: A long list remains in the main content rather than being kept short or moved to a separate page or appendix.
when: Long lists may be placed on a separate page or in an appendix.
The page gives a separate, explicit 25-word limit for lists running on from a phrase lead-in.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the long-list remedy with the length rule; E-4 prevents inventing a numerical threshold.

covers.quote: Content with too many lists is hard to follow. The content should flow so people can read it easily.

rules.quote: Limit the number of lists
rules.specification: No maximum count or density of lists is specified. The explanation makes readability and flow the basis for judging excess.
rules.violation_condition: A document contains so many lists that its flow is difficult to follow.
rules.why: The heading states a document-level constraint; E-4 prevents substituting an invented list-count limit.

covers.quote: Write items in a list so they follow a consistent pattern.
The pattern is made up by the number of words you use and grammatical structure.

rules.quote: Use a consistent pattern for list items
rules.specification: This item captures the paragraph's word-count aspect of a consistent pattern. Grammatical parallelism is inventoried separately. The manual gives no permitted variation in item length and does not require identical word counts.
rules.violation_condition: List items have inconsistent lengths that break the list's consistent pattern.
rules.why: G-4 absorbs the repeated instruction; the grain test separates length consistency from the independently stated grammatical check.

covers.quote: Write all list items so they have the same grammatical structure.
To make a parallel structure, use the same:
word type to start each item (such as a noun or a verb)

examples.note: The fragment-list items begin in lower case.

parts.quote: Writers should become familiar with the conventional types of content structure:

tags.violation_condition: A sentence-list or stand-alone-list item starts in lower case, or a fragment-list item starts with a capital despite not beginning with a proper noun.

when: Sentence-list and stand-alone-list items start with a capital letter.
Fragment-list items start in lower case unless the first word is a proper noun.
rules.why: G-2 combines list-type-dependent initial case in one check and records the proper-noun exception.

anchor.quote: Align run-over lines with the text, not the bullet or number.

tags.violation_condition: A run-over line in a sentence-list item aligns with its bullet or number rather than with the item's text.

when: Applies to sentence lists with items that wrap onto another line.
rules.why: This is a separate observable text-alignment property, not a repetition of punctuation or grammatical rules.

anchor.quote: Avoid using multiple sentences in each bullet or numbered item.
anchor.suffix: If you include more than one se

covers.prefix: n each bullet or numbered item.
covers.quote: If you include more than one sentence per list item, consider whether:
all list items conform to a similar pattern
the list builds rhythm for readability.

examples.note: Each numbered item contains one sentence.

parts.quote: The secretary will respond to each recommendation.
The secretary will allocate responses that need more work to members.
Members will discuss the recommendations at the next meeting on 9 March.

examples.note: The sentence lead-in is separate from the single-sentence items.

parts.quote: The committee members decided on several actions.
The secretary will respond to each recommendation.
The secretary will allocate responses that need more work to members.
Members will discuss the recommendations at the next meeting on 9 March.

tags.specification: Treat multiple sentences as discouraged rather than absolutely forbidden. The following advice identifies similar item patterns and readable rhythm as considerations, but supplies no hard acceptance test.
tags.violation_condition: A bullet or numbered item contains multiple sentences without maintaining a similar pattern across items and readable rhythm.

when: The instruction occurs under sentence lists.
More than one sentence per item is contemplated when items retain a similar pattern and the list builds readable rhythm.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the qualification with the discouragement; G-5 does not turn the writer's consideration process into another check.

anchor.quote: Use full sentence list items for imperative list items where there is no stated subject in the lead-in.

covers.quote: Use fragment list items when the lead-in states the grammatical subject.

examples.note: The imperative items receive sentence treatment because the phrase lead-in supplies no subject.

parts.quote: Learn about the words people use.
Choose simple words, not complicated expressions.

tags.specification: A subject stated in the lead-in means a subject grammatically shared with the items, not merely any subject appearing in an independent introductory sentence.
tags.violation_condition: Imperative items without a grammatical subject supplied by the lead-in are treated as fragments, or items continuing a subject supplied by the lead-in are treated as independent sentence items.

when: Imperative items with no stated subject in the lead-in receive full-sentence treatment.
Items continuing the grammatical subject in the lead-in receive fragment treatment.
This lead-in distinction does not classify stand-alone lists introduced by headings.
rules.why: G-2 combines the complementary subject-sharing cases into one item-type decision.

anchor.quote: Make sure each fragment can complete a phrase lead-in.

covers.quote: The last rule for fragment lists means that if you add each fragment to a phrase lead-in, it will make a complete sentence.
Fragment list items complete phrase lead-ins to form a grammatical sentence.

examples.note: Each fragment completes the phrase lead-in.
The manual identifies the second and third items as incompatible with the phrase lead-in.

parts.quote: the wildlife. It can kill you.

tags.violation_condition: Combining a fragment-list item with its phrase lead-in fails to produce a complete grammatical sentence.

when: Applies to fragment lists with a phrase lead-in.
Each item is tested separately with the lead-in.
rules.why: G-4 absorbs the explanations; E-3 preserves each complete list example.

anchor.prefix: the list should be very short.
anchor.quote: The full sentence should be 25 words or less.

covers.quote: If list items run-on from a phrase lead-in, the list should be very short.

tags.specification: Interpret the full sentence as the phrase lead-in plus all the run-on list items read as one sentence, rather than counting each lead-in–item pairing separately. The page does not explicitly resolve that counting distinction.
tags.violation_condition: A list running on from a phrase lead-in forms a full sentence longer than 25 words.

when: Applies when list items run on from a phrase lead-in.
rules.why: G-4 uses the explicit 25-word wording instead of a second vague shortness rule; E-4 exposes the counting interpretation.

anchor.quote: Items cannot be full sentences.

covers.quote: Items in stand-alone lists can be nouns or noun phrases.
covers.suffix: They can also be sentence fragm

covers.prefix: s can be nouns or noun phrases.
covers.quote: They can also be sentence fragments.
Stand-alone list items do not form a grammatical sentence.

examples.note: The manual presents these task phrases as stand-alone items.

tags.specification: The page treats verb-initial task phrases such as its weekly-task items as stand-alone fragments. Do not classify such phrases as prohibited full sentences solely because they could also be read as imperatives.
tags.violation_condition: A stand-alone list contains full-sentence items rather than nouns, noun phrases or sentence fragments.

when: Applies to stand-alone lists.
Nouns, noun phrases and sentence fragments are allowed.
rules.why: G-3 keeps the allowed forms with the prohibition; the example prevents overreading imperative-looking task phrases.

anchor.quote: Indent most lists

covers.quote: Indent most types of lists after the lead-in.
Indent stand-alone lists if it helps the user scan the list.
Indent each list item if it helps people scan the content.

tags.specification: The explicit exception concerns stand-alone lists. The page does not exhaustively define 'most' or provide an objective test for when indentation helps scanning.
tags.violation_condition: A list following a lead-in is not indented, or a stand-alone list is not indented where indentation is needed to help users scan it.

when: Indent lists after their lead-in.
Stand-alone lists need indentation only if it helps users scan the content.
rules.why: G-2 makes stand-alone indentation a condition of the same formatting check; G-4 absorbs repetitions.

anchor.quote: Ideally, lists of the same type should follow the same format, particularly when they appear close together in your content.
anchor.suffix: For example, a fragment list sh

covers.quote: Aim to write lists that conform to their type
For example, a fragment list should look the same as other fragment lists.

covers.prefix: ns this is not always possible.
covers.quote: For example, the logical flow of text can mean that some sentence lists work best with a sentence lead-in and others with a fragment lead-in.
For stand-alone lists, follow the same format for all list items – with indent/bullets or without indent/bullets.
Use the same symbol, number or letter for the same level in each list.

tags.specification: Use this check for cross-list presentation consistency, not to issue additional findings for case, full stops or sentence-lead-in punctuation already checked separately. For multilevel lists, 'same symbol, number or letter' means the same marker form or numbering system at a level, not repeating the same numeric value.
tags.violation_condition: Lists of the same type use inconsistent formatting without a content-driven reason, including inconsistent stand-alone indentation or bullets, or inconsistent marker forms for the same multilevel-list level.

when: Compare lists of the same type, especially nearby lists.
Logical flow can justify different sentence or phrase lead-ins for sentence lists.
Stand-alone lists should consistently use indentation and bullets, or consistently omit them.
The marker form for a given multilevel-list level should be consistent across lists.
rules.why: G-2 combines cross-list consistency cases and the content-flow exception; G-4 avoids separate findings for the specific restatements.

anchor.quote: Write numbered lists if the order is critical

covers.quote: Use a numbered (ordered) list when the order is important, such as a list of instructions.
Use an unordered list if the order is not critical to understanding the content.

examples.note: The page says users must complete these numbered steps in turn.

parts.quote: How to register for the conference:
Choose the days you will attend.
Pick the workshops you want to join.
Enter your discount code (if you have one).

tags.violation_condition: An order-critical list is not numbered, or a list whose order is not critical to understanding is presented as numbered rather than unordered.

when: Use a numbered list when order matters, such as instructions that must be completed in sequence.
Use an unordered list when order is not critical to understanding.
An unordered list can still be arranged alphabetically or in another helpful sequence.
rules.why: G-2 treats critical and non-critical order as complementary conditions for one list-marker choice.

anchor.quote: Avoid using in-line numbered lists

covers.quote: Break up text into a numbered list instead of using an in-line numbered list.

examples.note: The items are a displayed numbered list.
The numbered items are embedded in the sentence.

parts.quote: The facilitator will 1) welcome participants to the conference, and 2) introduce each of the speakers.

tags.violation_condition: Numbered items are embedded in running text instead of presented as a displayed numbered list.

rules.why: G-4 treats the body instruction as the remedy for the heading's prohibition; E-3 preserves the displayed list.

anchor.quote: To order points in general content, don’t use ordinal numbers.

covers.quote: use a numbered list
rephrase the sentences to link them in the same paragraph.

examples.note: The prose links the sequence with ‘Next’ rather than ordinals.

parts.quote: The facilitator will welcome participants to the conference. Next, they will introduce each of the speakers.

examples.note: The manual explicitly rejects the ordinal sequencing.

parts.quote: The facilitator will firstly welcome participants to the conference. Secondly, they will introduce each of the speakers.

tags.violation_condition: General prose uses ordinals such as ‘firstly’ and ‘secondly’ to sequence points.

when: Applies to ordering points in general content, not to expressing actual ranks.
A numbered list or linked sentences in the same paragraph are allowed alternatives.
rules.why: The ordinary paragraph following the example label states a new rule; G-3 keeps its permitted alternatives with that rule.

anchor.quote: Put unordered lists in a sequence that helps the user

covers.quote: List items in the order that will make sense to the user reading it.
covers.suffix: It’s common to write lists in a

covers.prefix: e sense to the user reading it.
covers.quote: It’s common to write lists in alphabetical order.

covers.prefix: he same list of national parks.
covers.quote: For example, you could also sort them by proximity to Perth.

examples.note: The manual identifies the alphabetical sequence as helpful while allowing context-dependent alternatives.

tags.specification: Alphabetical order is an example, not a universal requirement. Choosing the helpful order depends on the user's purpose and context.
tags.violation_condition: An unordered list is arranged in a sequence that does not make sense for the user's purpose.

when: Applies to unordered lists.
Alphabetical order is common.
Context may justify another sequence, such as geographic proximity.
rules.why: G-2 keeps context-dependent ordering choices together; E-1 does not turn a different sensible order into a violation.

anchor.quote: Avoid using a multilevel list

covers.quote: Some types of content need multilevel lists, but they can be hard for people to follow.

tags.specification: The page acknowledges that some content needs multilevel lists but does not specify which content qualifies.
tags.violation_condition: Content uses a multilevel list when the hierarchy is not needed.

when: Multilevel lists are allowed when the content needs a hierarchy.
Necessary multilevel lists remain subject to the depth and marker rules.
rules.why: G-3 records necessary multilevel lists as an exception; the specific requirements for allowed multilevel lists remain separate checks.

anchor.quote: Don’t use more than 2 levels.

tags.violation_condition: A multilevel list has three or more levels.

when: Applies when a multilevel list is used.
rules.why: The depth cap is independently testable even when using a multilevel list is justified.

anchor.quote: Use lowercase letters for the second level in a numbered list.

tags.violation_condition: Second-level markers in a numbered list use something other than lowercase letters.

when: Applies to the second level of a multilevel numbered list.
rules.why: This is the specific second-level marker check for numbered lists, distinct from depth and cross-list consistency.

anchor.quote: Use a dash for the second level in a bullet list, not hollow (open) bullets.

examples.note: The second-level markers are dashes.

parts.quote: There are many types of birds in Australia, including:

examples.note: The manual labels this nested-bullet version ‘Not this’; the marker difference is represented by list formatting rather than characters in the item text.

parts.quote: There are many types of birds in Australia, including:

tags.violation_condition: Second-level items in a bullet list use hollow bullets or another marker instead of a dash.

when: Applies to the second level of a multilevel bullet list.
rules.why: The manual's contrast tests second-level bullet markers; E-3 keeps the lead-in and all nested items together.
